newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - Dlr/mark vols subdued as spot pulls back.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Dlr/mark vols subdued as spot pulls back.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar/mark options were subdued in U.S. trading as spot pulled back from its early highs, dealers said.
Still, the dollar has been ratcheting up to new heights each day this week, and dealers said they were somewhat puzzled by the overall decline in volatility levels in the past few days.

"The dollar's basically at three-year highs...and risk reversals favor the upside, so you would assume a logical man would believe vols would be higher than they were yesterday," said Ted Voorhees, senior trader at Deutsche Bank in New York.

One-month dollar/mark implied volatility stood at 10.1/10.3 percent at U.S. midsession, roughly unchanged from late Wednesday levels but off slightly from highs earlier today, when the dollar climbed to a fresh 34-month high above 1.72 marks.
"As soon as spot started coming off, bids disappeared,' said a U.S. bank dealer in New York.

Risk reversals, which reflect pricing differential between puts and calls, stayed well skewed for mark puts, reflecting widespread expectation of a higher dollar. One-month 25-delta was around 0.3/0.6 percent.
Traders said the subdued volatility levels seemed especially odd because it was just one day before Friday's U.S. February employment report.
"The easy answer to that is exotic structures," Voorhees said. "There seems to be barriers between here and 1.74 (marks)."

Bank dealers who have sold exotic options, such as knockouts, to end-users have high time-decay risks. They tend to sell short-dated vanilla options until spot breaches the barriers and wipes out those exotics, forcing them suddenly to reverse and cover the short positions in the vanillas.
Voorhees was skeptical of the theory that traders had anticipated a higher dollar and had been long the upside strikes for some time.

"Perhaps...those options are now becoming at-the-money and they're paying time-decay," he said. At-the-money options have the highest theta value and are vulnerable to time decay. "But I find that hard to believe. Why unload before an important number like the employment report?"
Dollar/yen volatilities became bid as the dollar dipped toward 121.00 yen late in the U.S. morning, but were still down from Wednesday as spot was still within familiar ranges.
One-month volatility was off a quarter point at 10.6/10.9 percent at U.S. midsession. One-month 25-delta risk reversal stood at 0.0/0.3 percent in favor of yen calls.
Mark/yen volatilities were little changed, with the curve staying relatively steeply inverted, as the mark edged lower to fresh nine-month lows in the mid-70 yen area.
One-month mark/yen volatility stood at 10.1/10.4 percent, virtually unchanged.
Dealers said there was not as much buying in the 68-69 yen strikes as there had been earlier in the week, but that most traders appeared to believe the mark had some more downside.
